individuals of a long-lived marine predator increased their foraging effort in winter to overcome seasonal declines in prey availability.

1) individuals greatly increased their daily foraging time in overwintering, 2) foraging time was correlated to subsequent breeding phenology and, 3) the effect of foraging time was stronger in females than in males.

the effects of environmental and intrinsic factors (e.g. body condition and foraging efficiency) on the timing of breeding in long-lived birds.
the relationship between the environment and the behaviour of animals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the winter foraging and the breeding phenology of European shags is influenced by a number of intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
(1) winter phenology of a temperate seabirder is driven by intrinsic foraging ability and extrinsic weather conditions and food availability.
the European shag is a diurnal forager, that it forages for a greater proportion of the day in winter than in summer and that it does so to increase its energy intake.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the shags are not able to increase their foraging time to the maximum possible, which is limited by the weather conditions.
the intrinsic ability of shags to acquire food is a critical determinant of their overwintering forage time.
shags are able to increase foraging time in response to winter conditions and, in doing so, are able to maintain breeding phenology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the timing of the onset of breeding is a function of both extrinsic and intrinsic factors.

the timing of breeding in long-lived species is determined by the interaction of intrinsic and environmental factors, and that intrinsic ability to acquire resources is a key determinant of breeding phenology in the wild.
